passages.happening:
When Israel has settled in the land, it is to set apart three cities, divide the land into three regions, and build roads to them, ‘so that any manslayer can flee to these cities’ (verses 2-3).

Moses gives an example of who they are for. A man goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood. He swings his axe, ‘but the blade flies off the handle and strikes and kills his neighbor’ (verse 5). That man may flee to one of the cities and live. Otherwise ‘the avenger of blood might pursue the manslayer in a rage’ and kill him, ‘though he did not deserve to die’ (verse 6).

If God enlarges the land, three more cities are to be added (verses 8-9). “Thus innocent blood will not be shed in the land” (verse 10).

The cities are not for murderers. If a man hates his neighbor, lies in wait and kills him, and then runs to one of the cities, the elders of his own town must bring him back and hand him over (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
In the tribal societies of the ancient world there was no police force. A family defended its own. When someone was killed, the nearest male relative had the duty of avenging the death. He is called here ‘the avenger of blood’.

The danger is easy to see. In the heat of grief a relative might treat an accident as a murder, and a killing done in revenge could start a feud that ran for generations. Israel's law does not remove the avenger. It surrounds him with a legal process.

The case of the axe works like a small story with a point. No one hated anyone. Two neighbors went to work together, a tool failed, and one of them is dead. The law uses the picture to mark the difference between an accident and a murder. What matters is whether there was hatred and a plan.

Notice the care taken over the roads and the three regions. A refuge too far away is no refuge. The cities were to be within reach of every part of the land, with a clear way to them. Verse 6 names the very thing the law fears: that the distance will be too great and an innocent man will be caught and killed.

The Hebrew word for the avenger is go'el, the family's protector. He was the relative who bought back land that had been sold, and who bought a family member out of slavery. The same word is used of God as the Redeemer of his people.

The law protects in two directions. The man who killed by accident is kept alive. The man who murdered cannot hide behind the walls of the city. ‘Show him no pity’ in verse 13 guards the victim. It is aimed at the temptation to let a guilty man go because he is well connected or because the matter is awkward.

‘Innocent blood’ is a weighty phrase in this book. The shedding of it stains the whole land. A community is responsible for the deaths it could have prevented.

The note on Numbers 35 sets out the fuller law, including the question of the death penalty, on which Christians differ. Nothing in this law permits anyone today to take revenge for a death.
passages.later:
Numbers describes how the refuge worked: “The assembly is to protect the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood” (Numbers 35:25).

The book of Joshua names the six cities that were set apart, three on each side of the Jordan (Joshua 20:7-8).

The letter to the Hebrews borrows the picture for those who trust God's promise: ‘we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us’ (Hebrews 6:18). The New Testament does not call Jesus a city of refuge, and the picture should not be pressed further than that.
passages.asks: Israel was told to build the roads before anyone needed them. Ask what your community has in place for a person in sudden trouble, and whether it can be reached in time. And ask whether, when you hear that someone has done harm, you take the trouble to learn if it was meant.

passages.happening: One verse stands by itself. “You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker, which was set up by your ancestors to mark the inheritance you shall receive in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The edges of a family's field were marked with stones. To move a stone a little way at night was an easy way to steal land, and it was hard to prove. It was most easily done to a weak neighbor: a widow, an orphan, or a family with no one to speak for it.

In Babylonia, boundary stones sometimes carried written curses on anyone who shifted them.

In Israel the matter went deeper than property. The land was God's gift, shared out by tribe and by family. Each family's plot was its share in the promise. To move the marker was to steal from a neighbor and to show contempt for what God had given. A family that lost its land lost its living and its place.

The same Hebrew word is used in verse 8 for the borders of the whole land and here for the edge of one field. The promise to the nation and the protection of one small farm belong together.

The law is placed between a law about life and a law about truthful witness. All three protect a person from being wronged by someone stronger or more cunning.
passages.later:
The book of Proverbs repeats the law and names who is most at risk: “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you” (Proverbs 23:10-11).

The prophet Hosea used the picture for rulers who took what was not theirs: “The princes of Judah are like those who move boundary stones” (Hosea 5:10).
passages.asks: A boundary stone is moved a little at a time, at night, against someone who cannot fight back. Ask where you gain by small steps at the cost of a person who cannot easily object: in business, in a family matter, or in what you claim as yours.

passages.happening:
The rule of witnesses is given for every kind of case. “A lone witness is not sufficient to establish any wrongdoing or sin against a man, regardless of what offense he may have committed. A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (verse 15).

Then the case of a false witness. If someone accuses another of a crime, both must ‘stand in the presence of the LORD, before the priests and judges’ (verse 17). The judges are to investigate thoroughly. If the witness is shown to be a liar, “you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother” (verse 19).

The chapter ends with a formula. “You must show no pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, and foot for foot” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 17 the rule of two or three witnesses was given for cases that carried death. Here it is widened to ‘any wrongdoing’. No one in Israel could be found guilty of anything on one person's word.

A trial was held at the town gate, with elders, priests and judges. Verse 17 says the two parties stand ‘in the presence of the LORD’. A court was understood to sit before God himself. Lying there was lying to him.

The punishment of the false witness is exact. Whatever he tried to bring on the other person falls on him. If he accused a man of a crime that carried a fine, he pays the fine. If he tried to have a man put to death, he has tried to kill with words, and the law treats it so. This gave lying in court the weight of the crime it tried to create.

In a world where courts depended almost wholly on what witnesses said, the false witness was one of the most dangerous people in a town. The commandment against false witness forbids him. This law gives that commandment teeth.

‘Show no pity’ here again protects the victim, the one falsely accused.

The formula of verse 21, ‘eye for eye’, is taken up in the hard question below.
passages.later:
The books of Kings tell how Queen Jezebel had an innocent man killed by exactly this means. Two men were set up to accuse Naboth, and ‘they took him outside the city and stoned him to death’ (1 Kings 21:13).

At the trial of Jesus this law was broken: “For many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent” (Mark 14:56).

Jesus quoted the formula of verse 21 and spoke to how his followers answer a personal wrong: “But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

Paul says the same: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard:
Does ‘eye for eye’ approve of revenge?

In its setting the formula is a rule for judges and not for private persons. It sets a limit on punishment. The penalty must fit the harm, no more and no less, and it must be the same for rich and poor. In a world where a family might answer an injury by killing the offender, that was a restraint on revenge and not a license for it.

Older law collections have rules of the same kind. The laws of Hammurabi of Babylon include them, but apply them differently according to the rank of the person injured. Israel's law uses one measure for everyone.

There is good evidence that the formula was not always carried out to the letter. Exodus 21 already replaces bodily retaliation with the freeing of an injured slave. Later Jewish interpretation, recorded in the Mishnah, understood the law to require payment for an injury and not the maiming of the offender. Here in Deuteronomy the formula is applied to a false witness, whose penalty matches the harm he meant to do.

When Jesus quotes it in Matthew 5, he is speaking against using the principle to justify paying back a personal wrong. He does not overturn fair punishment by courts.

Christians differ on how directly this rule should shape criminal justice today. Most agree that its core, justice that is measured and equal for all, remains sound. It gives no one a right to take revenge.
passages.asks: The law made the liar bear what he meant for another. Ask what your words have cost other people: a reputation, a job or a friendship. And when you are wronged, ask which you want, justice or revenge. The law allows the first and Jesus forbids the second.
